description: Composite group of four panels spanning microscopy, EDS mapping and tensile-property curves. (a) is a STEM/TEM micrograph (100 nm scale bar) in which a dark, roughly equiaxed particle is outlined by a dashed white contour in a faintly striated matrix. (b) is a carbon-count EDS map of the same particle (100 nm scale bar) with a Counts colour bar running from 6.00 (deep blue) to 136.00 (red); its red/yellow core is labelled "Profile of (Ti, V)C" and the surrounding halo "Carbon rich region". The remaining panels are the tensile plots of Fig. 7: an engineering stress–engineering strain curve (y = Engineering stress (MPa), 0–1200, ticks at 200; x = Engineering strain, 0.0–0.8) and a dual-axis true stress–true strain / strain hardening rate plot (left y = True stress (MPa), 0–4000; right y = Strain hardening rate (MPa), 0–4000; x = True strain, 0.0–0.5). Both carry the legend M1-SS, M1-30, M2-SS, M2-30. Together the EDS panels establish a (Ti,V)C particle with an associated carbon-rich halo, while the tensile plots show that the aged conditions (M1-30, M2-30) reach the highest strength, with ductility strongly reduced for M1-30 but largely retained for M2-30. The caption's (a)/(b) letters describe the curve panels, not the two micrographs.

observations.observation: Panel (a) is a STEM/TEM micrograph with a 100 nm scale bar showing one dark, roughly equiaxed particle outlined by a dashed white contour in a faintly striated matrix.
Panel (b) is an EDS carbon map with a 'Counts' colour bar spanning 6.00 (dark blue) to 136.00 (red), the highest carbon counts concentrated in the core of the mapped particle.
Panel (b) annotates the red/yellow core as 'Profile of (Ti, V)C' and the surrounding halo as 'Carbon rich region', and carries a 100 nm scale bar.
The engineering stress–strain plot has y-axis 'Engineering stress (MPa)' over 0–1200 and x-axis 'Engineering strain' over 0.0–0.8, with the legend M1-SS, M1-30, M2-SS and M2-30.

The dual-axis plot uses 'True stress (MPa)' (0–4000) on the left, 'Strain hardening rate (MPa)' (0–4000) on the right, and 'True strain' (0.0–0.5) on the x-axis, with the same M1-SS/M1-30/M2-SS/M2-30 legend.

In the engineering stress–strain plot the aged M2-30 (red solid) curve reaches the highest peak, near the 1100 MPa level around strain ~0.3, then falls steeply, while M1-30 (black solid) peaks lower and ends near strain 0.4.
M1-SS (black dotted) extends to the largest strain, dropping sharply beyond ~0.8 engineering strain, indicating the largest elongation among the four conditions.

The micrograph and EDS map panels are themselves lettered (a) and (b), the same letters the caption uses for the mechanical-property curves, so the supplied caption does not describe the two micrographs.
The caption states Fig. 7 shows (a) the engineering stress–engineering strain curve and (b) the true stress–true strain and strain hardening rate curves of the low-density steels.

The citing text states the yield strength of solution-treated M1 steel was approximately 430 MPa, increasing to 860 MPa after aging due to homogeneous κ-carbide precipitation, with elongation reduced to 40 %.
The citing text states solution-treated M2 steel had a yield strength ~200 MPa higher than M1, and aged M2 reached 884 MPa with only a slight decrease in elongation.

The citing text states the work-hardening rate curves show a significant reduction for aged M1 (solid vs dashed lines), whereas aged M2 maintains a work-hardening rate comparable to its solution-treated state (solid red vs dashed lines).

The strain-hardening-rate curves fall steeply from about 4000 MPa at low true strain, with M1-30 (black solid) settling to a plateau near 1500 MPa while the true-stress curves rise gradually toward 1000–2000 MPa.
